title: Acute kidney injury
blurb: Spot people at risk, recognise AKI from creatinine and urine output, and take the nursing actions NICE NG148 expects: dipstick, fluid balance, medicines review and escalation.
question: Mr Bennett, 79, has CKD and takes ramipril and furosemide. He was admitted with diarrhoea. His creatinine was 118 micromol/L yesterday and is 152 today, and he has passed 140 mL of urine in the last 7 hours (he weighs 70 kg). Does he meet the criteria for AKI?

teach.h: A sudden drop in kidney function
teach.body: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a sudden fall in kidney function over hours to days, shown by a rise in serum creatinine or a fall in urine output. It is common in acutely ill people, often preventable, and frequently caused by dehydration, sepsis, medicines or obstruction rather than primary kidney disease. Plain English: the kidneys are struggling because something around them has gone wrong, and the nurse is often first to see it in the fluid chart.

head: Criterion
Threshold
rows: Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours
teach.caption: Any one criterion is enough. Compare creatinine with the person's baseline, and measure it regularly (typically daily in hospital).

teach.h: Urine output: the nurse's early warning

items.label: below this for more than 6 hours = AKI

teach.caption: NICE asks for systems to recognise and respond to oliguria when the early warning score does not include urine output (NG148 1.2.2).

head: Conditions
Situations
Exposures
teach.caption: Also: diabetes, previous AKI, oliguria, cognitive impairment or reliance on a carer for fluids, obstruction, and deteriorating early warning scores.

teach.body: Dipstick the urine for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose as soon as AKI is suspected and document it. Start an accurate fluid balance chart and monitor urine output. Escalate using NEWS2 and the creatinine trend. Ask the prescriber and pharmacist to review medicines: consider stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis, and avoid nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs. Identify and record the cause.

teach.text: Furosemide does not treat AKI. NICE says do not routinely offer loop diuretics for AKI, and do not offer low-dose dopamine. Loop diuretics may be considered for fluid overload while awaiting renal replacement therapy or during recovery. More urine on the chart is not the same as a recovering kidney.

teach.caption: NICE NG148 recs 1.4.4–1.4.6. Upper tract obstruction is referred to urology; nephrostomy or stenting within 12 hours.

teach.h: Refer immediately for renal replacement therapy (NG148 1.5.8)
head: If not responding to medical treatment

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Bennett on the medical ward
teach.body: Mr Bennett, 79, weighs 70 kg. His creatinine rose from 118 to 152 micromol/L in 24 hours (a rise of 34) and he has passed 140 mL in 7 hours, below 35 mL an hour for more than 6 hours. Both mean AKI. The nurse dipsticks his urine, starts a fluid balance chart, recalculates NEWS2, and escalates. She asks for his ramipril and furosemide to be reviewed because of his diarrhoea, and makes sure no NSAID is given.

items: AKI: creatinine up 26 micromol/L in 48 h, or up 50% in 7 days, or urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 6 h.
At risk: CKD, heart failure, diabetes, sepsis, hypovolaemia, age 65+, nephrotoxic drugs, contrast.
Dipstick urine early; keep an accurate fluid balance chart; escalate oliguria.
Consider stopping ACEi/ARBs in diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis; avoid NSAIDs.
No routine loop diuretics or dopamine; refer for RRT if complications do not respond.

summary: You can now identify adults at risk of AKI and recognise it from creatinine or urine output criteria. You can also take the first nursing actions NICE expects, from urinalysis and fluid balance to medicines review, imaging and escalation for renal replacement therapy.

A.q: Mr Bennett's creatinine was 118 micromol/L yesterday and is 152 micromol/L today. Which statement is correct?
options: This is not AKI; it needs a 50% rise
This meets AKI criteria: a rise of 26+ in 48 h
This is not AKI unless urine output falls
AKI needs creatinine above 200 micromol/L
A.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.3.1: a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours detects AKI. His rise is 34.

whyNot.0: The 50% rise is a separate 7-day criterion; any one criterion is enough.
whyNot.2: Creatinine and urine output criteria stand alone; either detects AKI.
whyNot.3: There is no absolute creatinine threshold; it is the change from baseline that matters.

A.q: Mrs Ong weighs 60 kg. Which urine output, sustained for more than 6 hours, meets the NG148 criterion for AKI?
options: 40 mL per hour
35 mL per hour
25 mL per hour
30 mL per hour
A.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.3.1: urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours. For 60 kg that is below 30 mL/h, so 25 mL/h meets it.

whyNot.0: 40 mL/h is above 0.5 mL/kg/h for 60 kg.
whyNot.1: 35 mL/h is above 0.5 mL/kg/h for 60 kg.
whyNot.3: 30 mL/h equals 0.5 mL/kg/h; the criterion is below this.

A.q: AKI is suspected in Mr Rossi. Which nursing action does NICE NG148 recommend as soon as AKI is suspected?
options: Dipstick the urine and record it
Insert a urinary catheter
Give a 1 L fluid challenge
Give oral furosemide
A.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.4.2: perform urine dipstick testing for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose in all people as soon as AKI is suspected or detected, document results and act on them.

whyNot.1: Catheterisation is not routine and adds infection risk; it depends on clinical need.
whyNot.2: Fluids are prescribed after assessment of volume status, not as a fixed challenge.
whyNot.3: NICE says do not routinely offer loop diuretics to treat AKI.

B.q: Mrs Dawson takes ramipril and has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. Her creatinine is rising. Which medicine change should the nurse raise with the prescriber?
options: Starting ibuprofen for her cramps
Increasing ramipril to protect her kidneys
Temporarily stopping ramipril
Adding a loop diuretic
B.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.2.14: consider temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in people with diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis until their condition has improved and stabilised.

whyNot.0: NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and an AKI risk factor.
whyNot.1: Increasing an ACE inhibitor during dehydration worsens AKI risk.
whyNot.3: Loop diuretics are not used to treat AKI and add to volume loss.

B.q: Mr Hussain has AKI with no obvious cause. When should he have an ultrasound of the urinary tract?
options: Within 6 hours
Within 7 days
Within 1 hour
Within 24 hours
B.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.4.6: if there is no identified cause or a risk of obstruction, offer urgent ultrasound within 24 hours of assessment.

whyNot.0: 6 hours is for suspected pyonephrosis (infected, obstructed kidney).
whyNot.1: 7 days is too slow when no cause has been found.
whyNot.2: There is no 1-hour ultrasound standard in NG148.

B.q: Mrs Clarke has AKI. Her potassium remains 6.8 mmol/L and she is acidotic despite medical treatment. What should happen?
options: Repeat the bloods in 24 hours
Start low-dose dopamine
Refer immediately for renal replacement therapy
Give a loop diuretic to clear the potassium
B.why: NICE NG148 recs 1.5.8 and 1.5.11: refer immediately for renal replacement therapy if hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema do not respond to medical management.

whyNot.0: Persistent hyperkalaemia is life-threatening and cannot wait 24 hours.
whyNot.1: NICE says do not offer low-dose dopamine to treat AKI.
whyNot.3: Loop diuretics are not a treatment for AKI or refractory hyperkalaemia.

C.q: Mr Okoye, 72, has type 2 diabetes and heart failure and is due a contrast CT. His eGFR is 26. He takes metformin, ramipril and furosemide. Which action best reduces his AKI risk?
options: Give the scan without changes to avoid delay
Discuss pausing ramipril and plan hydration
Add a regular NSAID for back pain first
Double his furosemide on the day
C.why: NICE NG148 recs 1.2.7–1.2.9: encourage oral hydration, consider IV volume expansion for inpatients at particularly high risk (such as eGFR below 30), and consider temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in adults with CKD and eGFR below 30 having iodinated contrast.

whyNot.0: He has several risk factors (CKD, heart failure, diabetes, ACE inhibitor), so prevention is needed.
whyNot.2: NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and raise AKI risk.
whyNot.3: Extra diuretic before contrast increases hypovolaemia and AKI risk.

C.q: Mrs Field, 84, lives with dementia and relies on her carer for drinks. She has a UTI and her NEWS2 is rising. Which statement about her AKI risk is most accurate?
options: Dementia and carer reliance are AKI risk factors
AKI risk is low because she has no CKD
Her risk rises once she is 90 or older
UTI does not affect her AKI risk
C.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.1.1: cognitive impairment or disability limiting access to fluids, sepsis, deteriorating early warning scores and age 65+ are all AKI risk factors.

whyNot.1: CKD is one risk factor of many; she has several others.
whyNot.2: The NG148 age risk factor starts at 65.
whyNot.3: Infection leading to sepsis and a deteriorating NEWS2 both raise risk.

C.q: Mr Lane's AKI is clearly due to dehydration from gastroenteritis and his creatinine is falling quickly with IV fluids. A student asks if he needs a nephrology referral. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, everyone with AKI needs one
Yes, and an ultrasound within 6 hours
Yes, as his creatinine has risen
No, not when the cause is clear and improving
C.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.5.12: do not refer to a nephrologist when there is a clear cause for AKI and it is responding promptly to medical management (unless the person has a renal transplant). Rec 1.4.4: no routine ultrasound when the cause is known.

whyNot.0: NG148 advises against referral in clear-cause, responding AKI.
whyNot.1: Ultrasound within 6 hours is for suspected pyonephrosis.
whyNot.2: A creatinine rise defines AKI but does not itself require nephrology referral.

reteach.title: Pre, intra, post: where is the kidney being hurt?
reteach.question: Think of the kidney as a factory with a delivery road in and a drain out. What can go wrong at each point, and what does the nurse do?

blocks.body: Road in: low blood supply from dehydration, bleeding, sepsis, or drugs such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics. Restore volume and review medicines. Factory: damage from nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast) or nephritis (blood and protein on dipstick with no other cause). Drain out: obstruction, so scan within 24 hours if no cause is found. The nurse's tools are the fluid chart, the dipstick, the creatinine trend and NEWS2.

blocks.text: 26 in 48 hours, 50% in 7 days, 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Any one of the three is AKI.

explain.body: Creatinine rise of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours, a 50% or greater rise within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours.

test.q: A woman's baseline creatinine 5 days ago was 70 micromol/L; today it is 110. Does this meet AKI criteria?
options: No, the rise is over 48 hours
Yes, it has risen 50% or more in 7 days
No, it is below 120
Yes, because it is above 100
test.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.3.1: a 50% or greater rise within 7 days. 70 to 110 is a 57% rise.

whyNot.0: The 7-day percentage criterion applies even though the 48-hour window has passed.
whyNot.2: There is no fixed upper value; the change from baseline matters.
whyNot.3: An absolute value of 100 is not a criterion.

explain.body: CKD (eGFR below 60), heart failure, liver disease, diabetes, previous AKI, oliguria, cognitive impairment or reliance on carers for fluids, hypovolaemia, nephrotoxic drugs in the past week, contrast, obstruction, sepsis, deteriorating EWS, age 65+.

test.q: Which medicine taken in the past week is listed by NICE as a risk factor for AKI?
options: Paracetamol
Lansoprazole
Ibuprofen
Salbutamol
test.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.1.1: NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen), aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics are listed.

whyNot.0: Paracetamol is not on the NG148 list.
whyNot.1: PPIs are not on the NG148 list.
whyNot.3: Salbutamol is not on the NG148 list.

explain.body: Urine dipstick as soon as AKI is suspected. Fluid balance and urine output monitoring. Escalate oliguria. Medicines review with a pharmacist; consider stopping ACEi/ARBs in diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis. Record the cause.

test.q: A man with AKI has haematuria and proteinuria on dipstick, no catheter and no UTI. What does NICE suggest considering?
options: Acute nephritis and nephrology referral
A repeat dipstick in a month
Starting a loop diuretic
Encouraging 3 L of oral fluid a day
test.why: NICE NG148 rec 1.4.3: think about acute nephritis and nephrology referral when there is no obvious cause and the dipstick shows blood and protein without infection or catheter trauma.

whyNot.1: A month's delay could miss a treatable nephritis.
whyNot.2: Loop diuretics do not treat AKI.
whyNot.3: A fixed high fluid intake does not address nephritis and may cause overload.

explain.body: No routine loop diuretics, no low-dose dopamine. Refer immediately for RRT when hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema do not respond.

test.q: When may loop diuretics be considered in AKI, according to NICE?
options: As routine treatment to restore output
For fluid overload while awaiting RRT
To prevent AKI before contrast
Whenever urine output is below 0.5 mL/kg/h
test.why: NICE NG148 recs 1.5.3–1.5.4: do not routinely offer loop diuretics; consider them for fluid overload or oedema while awaiting RRT or during recovery.

whyNot.2: Diuretics increase AKI risk before contrast.
whyNot.3: Oliguria alone is not an indication; it needs the cause treated.
